title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: a still room, no draft, and a baby breathing. The hymn's second verse: before day and night, That One breathed without wind
carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's first verse: not non-being, not being, no air, no sky, and then only questions. Did you ask one more question before rushing to an answer? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

A small room late at night. The window is shut. The fan is off. Not a curtain moves. In a crib in the corner, a baby is asleep, and the only motion in the whole room is the rise and fall of that tiny chest. Lean close and there's the faintest sound of breath. No wind is blowing anywhere. Nothing pushes that breath from outside. It comes from within, all by itself, steady and quiet. A parent can stand there a long time, just listening. The Nasadiya Sukta's second verse reaches for something like that stillness, before there was a night to fall asleep in, and finds a breath.
screen: `A STILL ROOM. NOTHING MOVES.` → `ONE SMALL BREATH.` → `FROM WITHIN, BY ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's verse cleared away being and non-being, air and sky. The second verse keeps clearing. In paraphrase: there was no death then, and no deathlessness. There was no sign to tell night from day. Notice what's gone now. Death and its opposite, the undying. Gone. Night and day, the rhythm a life runs on. Gone, or not yet. And then, for the first time in the hymn, something is. That One breathed, the verse says, without wind, by its own power. Apart from it, there was nothing else at all. Look at the words. Not a god with a name. Not Agni, not Indra, not Varuna. Just That One, tad ekam. And not doing anything grand. It breathes. Breath is life, but here there's no air for breathing, so the breath is windless, moved by nothing outside itself. Readers have taken That One in different ways. Vedanta teachers in Shankara's line hear Brahman, prior to every name. Other Hindu readers hear the Lord before the work of creation. Some hear a poet pushing language as far as it will go and finding only a breath. The verse doesn't decide for them. And notice: no questions in this verse. After yesterday's flood of them, the hymn pauses on one quiet claim. The questions will come back. For now, a breath in the stillness.
screen: `NO DEATH, NO DEATHLESSNESS.` · `NO SIGN OF NIGHT OR DAY.` · `THAT ONE BREATHED, WITHOUT WIND.` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a breath that moves by itself. Sit, and stop managing the breath. Don't deepen it, don't slow it. Just let it go on its own and watch. Notice that nothing outside is pushing it. It rises. It falls. Rest in the stillness around it, like a quiet room at night. When your mind starts to explain the breath, let the explanation go and come back to the plain fact of it. If you pray, you can rest in that breath as a gift. The bell holds the time.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation, whose second verse says: no death, no deathlessness, no night or day, only That One, breathing without wind. Today's word.

Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? Today, when a room goes still, a parked car, a light switched off, listen once for the breath that keeps going on its own. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Nasadiya Sukta's 'That One' (tad ekam) in different ways: in Advaita Vedanta as Brahman beyond names, in devotional schools as the Lord before creation, and it is chanted as part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

fork.setup: you're the poet. there's no air, no sky, no night or day, no death. is anything there at all? what do you write?
options: That One breathed, without wind, by its own power.
fork.reveal: the verse says That One breathed, windless, by its own power, and apart from it there was nothing else.

original.note: Sanskrit: tad ekam, That One. What the Nasadiya Sukta's second verse says breathed, without wind.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hymn of creation starts with a god at work.
what it means: its second verse names no god. That One breathes, without wind, before night and day.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 10.129.2, anid avatam svadhaya tad ekam, That One breathing windless by its own power, read by Vedanta as Brahman.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
